groups.reason: An invariant of the runtime's or the emitter's own bookkeeping: a task id that is not in the task table, a shard lock taken twice, a switch default over an id the emitter itself assigned. No Surge program can arrange these; a program that reached one would be evidence of a defect above it, not of the behaviour under test, so a fixture pinning the report would be pinning the wrong thing.
groups.invalidated_when: The condition becomes reachable from a Surge program - most plausibly because a runtime API is exposed to source, or a dispatch id starts coming from data rather than from the emitter.

groups.reason: An allocation-failure guard. Reaching it needs the allocator to answer NULL, which the corpus cannot arrange: it runs real programs against the real allocator and has no fault injection. The guard is still the right code - the alternative is dereferencing NULL - it simply cannot be provoked from a .sg file. One row is now provoked, by a build rather than by a fixture: SURGE_INTERNAL_TEST_ALLOC_REFUSAL names one emitted allocation site and the compiler asks for a size no allocator serves there, which TestRuntimeV2AllocationRefusalReportsTheTypeItCouldNotAllocate runs. That is native-only and is not a two-backend fixture, so the row stays here.
groups.invalidated_when: The corpus itself can make an allocation fail - a heap cap a fixture can set low enough, or an allocator the VM lane can refuse from too - at which point the report becomes an answer both backends can record.

groups.reason: A null-pointer guard, defence in depth. The emitter never passes NULL to these entry points, and the type system upstream of it does not admit a null array or string handle. The guard exists so that a future caller that got it wrong fails with a sentence instead of a segfault.
groups.invalidated_when: A caller outside the emitter can reach the entry point - an FFI surface, or a runtime API called from source - at which point NULL stops being impossible and the report becomes a real answer worth recording.

groups.reason: An arithmetic guard on a 64-bit length, capacity or stride. Reaching it needs a value near 2^63, which means either an allocation of that size - the machine refuses first - or a bignum with more limbs than the limit allows, which costs the same memory. The guard protects a multiplication that would otherwise wrap silently.
groups.invalidated_when: The limit stops being memory-sized: a configurable cap a fixture can lower, or a length that arrives from data rather than from an allocation the program already paid for.

groups.reason: An emitter guard on an operand the runtime ABI must receive as a 64-bit integer. Every one of these rows is the same helper - emitUintOperandToI64, emitIntOperandToI64, or the checked bignum narrowings under them - called with a different noun in its message. What differs between rows is the sentence, not the check, and the sentence is exactly what a wording drift would move; recording the sentence here is what makes such a move a reported finding rather than a silence.
groups.invalidated_when: A row's message stops being produced by the shared narrowing helper, or the helper stops being one implementation - at which point each caller is checking something of its own and wants its own fixture.

groups.reason: A crossing failure report: a destination shard that is shut down, a transport queue that is full, a lease that was already released. Reaching one needs a multi-shard program in a particular failure state, which the behavioural corpus - one worker, one process, comparing output byte for byte - is the wrong instrument for. These paths are exercised by the transport and crossing gates instead, which can arrange the failure.
groups.invalidated_when: The behavioural corpus learns to run a multi-shard program, or a crossing failure becomes reachable in the single-worker configuration the corpus uses.

groups.reason: The raise has no message of its own to record: it forwards text the program supplied, or a buffer the runtime formats at the moment of failure. There is no string here for a fixture to match, so coverage has to be asserted about the caller rather than about this site. Recording the site keeps it in the census; it is the one class where the ledger cannot also check a wording.
groups.invalidated_when: The site starts naming a fixed condition, at which point it has a message and belongs under one of the other dispositions.

groups.reason: Reachable from an ordinary Surge program, and no fixture reaches it. This is the backlog the gate exists to make visible, not an excuse: the right response to a row here is to write the fixture and delete the row, and the right response to a NEW panic site is never to add one. Every row here is a place where the two backends could already disagree and nothing would say so.
groups.invalidated_when: A fixture records the message on both backends - the gate then reports the row as redundant and it must be removed.
